analysis.title: AI Entrant Series: Proliferate or Participate? Public Transportation: TYL and IOT
key_insights: Third report in JPM's AI Entrant Series, covering Tyler Technologies (TYL) and Samsara (IOT) in public transportation, where the two companies overlap.

JPM found multiple smaller AI-native competitors rather than one or two names, which suggests a more fragmented market. It sees OpenGov and C3.ai as having the most potential read-through to both companies.

JPM's view is that the most credible threat to Tyler and Samsara is each other. Most large-scale industry-deployed AI is being built by these two companies, and smaller AI-native solutions are not gaining notable traction.

The overlap is in K-12 school bus transportation and municipal fleets. The open question is whether Tyler extends down-market into operational telemetry and safety workflows, or Samsara extends up-market into the government workflow layer.

Samsara is targeting the government and municipal vertical, often with competitive pricing concessions. Recent wins: a top-5 U.S. city expanded from one division to a multi-department rollout (fire, parks, public works, transit) with Ground Intelligence across 7,600 lane miles, plus State of California as connected operations platform, State of New York in late 2025, and First Student last year.
Samsara launched its Public Sector AI Suite in May 2026 (Ground Intelligence, Waste Intelligence, Ridership Management) and also launched AI Safety Coach and Agent Studio.

JPM sees Tyler's moat as 25+ years as the primary software provider to U.S. state and local governments, with over 15,000 jurisdictions, all 50 states and over 50,000 installations, and relationships of 20+ years.

Tyler's differentiation is its singular public-sector focus: School ERP Pro, Absence & Substitute Management, Enterprise Justice, the My Ride K-12 parent app (over 1M users) and property appraisal and tax systems.
Samsara's differentiation is hardware-linked: AI Multicam and 360 Camera, Ground Intelligence, Waste Intelligence, Asset Tag XS and gateways (6-year battery life) and the Samsara Wearable.

OpenGov is the most direct AI-native threat to both. Its platform combines ERP, budgeting, asset management, permitting and procurement and serves more than 2,000 agencies. JPM says it is winning head-to-head citywide ERP and financial software bids against Tyler.
OpenGov's overlap with Samsara is narrower and sits in enterprise asset management. In Kansas City its platform helped triple the road resurfacing rate and manage over 100,000 assets.

C3.ai is a horizontal agentic AI and data unification layer. Its threat to Tyler and Samsara is mostly conceptual, though it was selected by the U.S. Department of Agriculture for public engagement and inquiry processing.
Tegus expert calls point to a gap in Tyler's budgeting tool, which is more of a general ledger budgeting tool than a purpose-built one. OpenGov's budgeting offering targets that gap.
A former Tyler VP said Tyler pushes payments aggressively and reduced or removed APIs for third-party payment integrations, using payments as a control point and lock-in tactic.

Tegus calls on K-12 transportation show both Samsara and Tyler as core stack vendors. Tyler is strong in Texas and the upper East Coast, while Samsara is expanding across Washington, Oregon, Texas and the East Coast.
C3.ai's vulnerabilities per experts: long procurement cycles, no proprietary data moat, and no deep strategic partnerships, including with hyperscalers.

market_movers.rationale: JPM rates Tyler Overweight with a $525 target (set 23-Jun-26) and cites its installed base and relationships as structural defensibility. Price was $392.45 on 22 Oct 2026.
JPM rates Samsara Neutral with a $52 target (set 03-Sep-26). Price was $43.78 on 22 Oct 2026.

sector_views.rationale: AI-native entrants have had minimal competitive impact so far. JPM sees the main medium-term risk as Tyler and Samsara moving into each other's core buying centers.

risk_factors: Tyler and Samsara could move into each other's core buying centers (Tyler into operational and field data, Samsara into workflow and system of record), turning adjacency into head-to-head competition.
OpenGov is winning head-to-head citywide ERP and financial software bids against Tyler, and Tyler's budgeting tool is a known gap.
Samsara's use of pricing concessions in government deals could pressure its margins, and its gains in school transportation put pressure on Tyler's franchise there.
AI-native point solutions could scale, though JPM sees long sales cycles, legacy integrations, data governance constraints and workflow ownership politics as frictions.
C3.ai could eventually become competitive by unifying hardware data and software into one view.

tension_points.bull_case: Tyler and Samsara are embedding AI into production systems used daily. Smaller AI-native entrants are mostly point solutions with limited enterprise procurement wins, and face long sales cycles and legacy integration hurdles. Tyler's installed base and Samsara's hardware data capture provide moats.
tension_points.bear_case: OpenGov is winning head-to-head citywide ERP bids against Tyler. C3.ai could unify hardware and software data above both incumbents, and Tyler and Samsara may encroach on each other's buying centers.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence of OpenGov or C3.ai winning large-scale procurement deals in the Tyler and Samsara overlap zone, or Tyler and Samsara competing head-to-head for the same buying center.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI-native competitor impacts on Tyler and Samsara are minimal at this stage, so the strongest competitive threat is between the two.
theme_stances.evidence: AI-native competitor impacts on Tyler and Samsara are seemingly minimal at this stage
